Yes. several times. Since most of the stories so far have been from the point of view of shady pyramid schemes or fraud schemes looking for "employees" with little to no work experience, let me tell one that may occur a decade or two into your career.

A legitimate company (with no morals or ethics) places an ad or hires a staffing firm to find senior-level talent. (I work in IT, but this is not an IT-only story).

You show up in a suit, and get interviewed by several people, sometimes together, sometimes in succession. All is going well. Then they either have the "technical interview" where one manager presents a very detailed and complex problem and asks how you would resolve it. It appears they are testing your problem-solving skills and stated experience. Sometimes, instead, you are given the problem set as homework to be turned in a couple days later.

So everything looks good, right? You nailed the in-person, you nailed the problem-solving exercise. Nope. You are not going to get the job, because there IS NO JOB. Fuckers are too damn cheap to hire consultants, so they pretend to have a job opening and plan to get the solution to their problem through the interview process.

This happens in other industries, not just tech. Be warned. Learn to sense when you are being asked for far more information that is required for an interview. And then walk.

Yes. I once went to a job interview for a "martial arts instructor" position. It all started out pretty well, the guy asked me some generic sounding questions about why I'm interested in becoming a martial arts instructor, told me he liked me and my answers, and would like to offer me the job. He then went on to tell me what my "responsibilities" and "job role" would entail, which is where things started to unravel.

The job was actually door-to-door promotion and flyer distribution, earning commission on karate lesson subscriptions, while being given "free martial arts training". Then once you're "good enough" you'd start teaching classes full time because "you've brought in enough people that we'll need new teachers". You only start doing the martial arts training after you've sold a certain number of subscriptions however. In other words; you don't get free training. "However if you'd like to pay for it, you can receive the training much earlier".

The reality is that this is just a cynical exploitation of jobseekers in order to get some free advertising.

The dude who interviewed me put on a convincing act to make it seem like a legit busy dojo by jogging around the building (just a community center, they had no actual dojo of their own), doing "warmup" exercises, etc. while pretending he hasn't noticed us sitting in the car. Once the interview began, he tells me he's going to "keep it short, because I have a class in a few minutes". Little did he know that my dad had taken the car to go do other things while I was being interviewed, so I actually had to stand around and wait for quite a while outside after the interview. Nobody turned up for this "lesson", the guy sheepishly came out several times to check if I was still there, and on spotting me tried to make himself look like he was coming outside to do other things.

After my dad turned up, we talked in the car for a while about where he'd been and how the interview went. Still nobody showed up. Needless to say I never took the job.
